$comment: DNS page: receptionist analogy (resolver asks around: info desk -> town hall -> bakery, keeps a note for a while).

title.text: DNS: how a name becomes an address
title.subtitle: One resolver asks around, then remembers

sections.label: An everyday analogy: the receptionist

turns.says: Where is Example Bakery in Oakdale?
12 Mill Street. The bakery told me.
The next person gets it from my notes.

sections.intro: The receptionist follows the same routine every time:
rules: You ask one person. She does all the calling.
She calls the info desk, town hall, then bakery.
Only the bakery itself knows the address for sure.
Her note is good for one hour, then she asks again.

sections.label: The same routine in DNS
sections.text: Root and TLD servers only point onward. The resolver makes every call.

items.heading: Cache hit
items.text: Same name again? The resolver answers from memory, with no calls at all.

items.heading: TTL
items.text: Time to live, in seconds, set by the zone owner. 3600 is her one-hour note.

items.heading: Why changes lag
items.text: Change a record and old copies stay in caches until their TTL runs out.

items.heading: Many notebooks
items.text: Your browser and operating system keep their own copies too.

sections.label: What the bakery can answer: record types

items.heading: CNAME
items.text: An alias for another name. It can hold no other record types.

items.heading: MX
items.text: Which servers take mail. The lower number is tried first.

items.heading: TXT
items.text: Notes for machines: SPF mail rules, domain ownership checks.

items.heading: NS
items.text: The zone's authoritative servers. The TLD hands these out.

items.note: Asks your resolver. The number after the name is the TTL left. Windows has `nslookup` for this.
Walks root -> TLD -> authoritative by itself, like the receptionist.

sections.text: DNS servers listen on port 53, for both UDP and TCP.
bullets: **UDP**: everyday lookups, one packet each way
**TCP**: answers too big for UDP, and zone copies

sections.text: You ask one resolver. It asks root, TLD and the authoritative server, then keeps the answer until the TTL runs out.
